chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
title: The new owner's marital trouble and the fires
summary: The Florida buyer's wife set the club on fire twice over his affair with the barmaid; Durham opened his own club and played nine places.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: (Inaudible) but I did give him a contract that I would come in and supply if I wasn't in. So, he took it and he (inaudible). Had a lot of trouble with his wife. Then I

opened up a club out there myself out there, got a license. He was having so much trouble with his wife, this fella -- he was from Florida, white fella -- he was going with the barmaid, because he and his wife separated. Finally she come from Florida and she had a baby he had left and she come (inaudible) "This is trouble, trouble, trouble." I stayed right on top of it and I knew this woman was going to -- she come in there with a gun looking for him, you know, and he'd be just went out with that woman and I'd have to quit playing to get some of the guys to go find him. (Inaudible) wife yelling, "You got to do something about you and this girl." Well, this is my old lady now. So he got in a lot of trouble, got in a lot of trouble out there with his wife.

She set the place on fire again out there and the saxaphone player found it and she say, "I'm going to burn it down." Second time, see? So then he kept fooling around and the saxaphone player laid on it and she set it on fire again and I got Benny Glass the lawyer to go out there and kind of get him out of all that trouble, because he was in the oil business and the bakery business. Young fella from Florida.
So that's what I was doing during those days. I played about nine places out there. I played for Lisa's and
I had about five or six pieces. But I would only take about three nights a week.
